content: Measles, also known as rubeola, is an extremely contagious viral infection. The most effective protection against measles is achieved through two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provides weekly updates on the number of confirmed measles cases and outbreaks in the United States. The initial symptoms of measles typically appear 7 to 14 days after exposure to the virus. These symptoms include fever, cough, and a runny nose. Individuals planning to travel internationally should ensure they are vaccinated with the MMR vaccine to protect against measles, mumps, and rubella. The MMR vaccine is essential for preventing measles. It is important to understand the basics of the vaccine, including who should receive it, the appropriate timing for vaccination, and the reasons for its necessity. Educational resources about measles are available for download and distribution to increase awareness and understanding of the disease. For healthcare professionals, clinical guidelines are available to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of measles cases. Health departments can access critical resources, such as case definitions and protocols for managing outbreaks and implementing response measures. Laboratory confirmation of measles infection can be achieved through the detection of measles RNA using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing. Recommendations for the MMR vaccine include routine vaccination schedules, criteria for evidence of immunity, and other important considerations related to measles immunization.
